text: In 2017 Rutherford Chang said:
"I'm going to start hoarding pennies."
The penny, he said, is "the lowest common
denominator, it's like junk, it's like nothing."
He had, he said,
"no idea" what he would make of them.
What he made, CENTS, is a work of its medium.
Chang inscribed images of ten
thousand copper cents on Bitcoin,
and the work shows what happens
to money when its record passes
from a state to a public network
that anyone can read and no one runs.
Released at one satoshi each,
the inscriptions moved each cent's value
from a figure set by the state
into an ongoing process,
set and set again by the people
who keep, read and exchange each Cent.
It began with copper.
A copper cent struck before 1983
holds more than a cent's worth of copper.
Hoarding them, he said,
was like "buying 1.7 cents of copper
for one cent and it's still worth one cent."
Chang's statement for the work
begins from such "discrepancies in value."
He took ten thousand copper cents out
of circulation and photographed every coin.
Coins made to be identical turned out to differ,
each marked by its own wear, toning and color.
He had the coins melted and cast
into one block, CENTS Block Copper.
In March 2024 he inscribed
the image of each obverse,
one image to one satoshi,
the smallest unit of bitcoin,
and in April the block's model,
which fills a whole block of the chain:
CENTS Block 839969.
His statement calls it "an immutable
digital monument."
The coin, its image, its inscription,
the copper and the model:
each is a cent in its own way.
Collectors preferred the damaged to the clean.
A council of collectors reviewed and voted
on all ten thousand Cents three times,
and agreed on nineteen traits.
Chang's statement ends:
"its value can continue to be redefined
through this digitally scarce set of 10,000
and the block that encapsulates
their transformation."
